Check Unidimensionality and Monotonicity Before an Ordered Analysis

Source: R/26_ScaleCheck.R
MonotonicityCheck.Rd

Runs the checks that an order-restricted (isotonic) analysis takes for granted: that every item rises with the same latent order, with no reverse-keyed item left unrecoded and no item that peaks in the middle. For each item it reports the item-rest correlation, the loading on the first principal component, the scalability coefficient \(H_j\), and the violations of manifest monotonicity, and flags the items that look reverse-keyed, non-monotone or weak.

Usage

MonotonicityCheck(
  U,
  na = NULL,
  Z = NULL,
  w = NULL,
  fields = NULL,
  minvi = 0.03,
  minsize = NULL,
  weak_h = 0.3,
  max_rounds = NULL
)

Arguments

U

Either an object of class "exametrika" or raw data. When raw data is given, it is converted to the exametrika class with the dataFormat function.

na

Values to be treated as missing values.

Z

Missing indicator matrix of type matrix or data.frame. Values of 1 indicate observed responses, while 0 indicates missing data.

w

Item weight vector. Not used.

fields

Optional vector with one entry per item giving its subscale (field). NULL (default) treats all items as one scale.

minvi

Smallest decrease counted as a violation. Default 0.03.

minsize

Smallest rest-score group. NULL (default) uses the rule described in Details.

weak_h

Threshold of \(H_j\) below which an item is flagged as weak. Default 0.3.

max_rounds

Maximum number of rounds of the iteration. NULL (default) allows as many rounds as there are items.

Value

An object of class c("exametrika", "MonotonicityCheck") with

items

Data frame, one row per item: field, item, item-rest correlation, first-component loading, \(H_j\), number of violations, number of significant violations, largest \(z\), and the flags (all against the clean rest score of the final round).

fields

Data frame, one row per field: number of items and respondents used, \(H\) over all items, \(H\) over the items left unflagged, number of flagged items and rounds used.

rounds

List per field of the flagged items in each round.

detail

List per field of the rest-score group tables of the final round, as in ManifestMonotonicity.

minsize, minvi, weak_h

The settings used.

Details

Reference set and iteration. An item is judged against the rest score, but a reverse-keyed or non-monotone item inside the rest score distorts the yardstick for every other item, so that sound items also show violations. The rest score is therefore built from a reference set of items that is cleaned step by step. It starts from the items whose first-component loading has the majority sign. In each round every item is judged against the reference set (excluding itself); if an item in the set is flagged as reverse-keyed or non-monotone, the worst one (most significant violations, then lowest item-rest correlation) leaves the set and the round is repeated. Removing one item at a time keeps a heavily contaminated first round from discarding every item. The items outside the final set after each round are kept in rounds.

Subscales. When fields is given, each subscale is checked on its own. This matters: on a multidimensional scale the item-total relations are dominated by the mixture of dimensions, and reverse-keyed items can stay hidden when all items are pooled.

Flags. An item is flagged "reverse?" when its correlation with the clean rest score is negative, "non-monotone" when it has at least one significant violation of manifest monotonicity (see ManifestMonotonicity; with large samples even a small decrease becomes significant, so read the flag together with the number of violations and the largest \(z\)), and "weak" when \(H_j\) against the clean items is below weak_h (0.3, Mokken's rule of thumb). The first-component loading is computed once on all items of the subscale (tetrachoric or polychoric correlations) and reported for reference; its sign is oriented to sum to a positive value, so it marks items against the majority rather than against a known direction.

Respondents with a missing response in a subscale are dropped for that subscale. The function only reports; recoding or dropping items is left to the person who prepares the data.

See also

Scalability, ManifestMonotonicity, Dimensionality

Examples

# \donttest{
mc <- MonotonicityCheck(J5S1000)
#> MonotonicityCheck: 26 respondents with missing responses were dropped for field 'All'.
mc
#> Unidimensionality and Monotonicity Check
#> minvi = 0.03, weak if Hj < 0.3
#> 
#> Field All: 5 items, 974 respondents, H = 0.245 (unflagged items: 0.245), 1 round(s)
#>  Item r_rest loading    Hj n_violation n_significant z_max flag
#>    V1  0.336   0.611 0.234           1             0 0.597 weak
#>    V2  0.367   0.685 0.259           0             0 0.000 weak
#>    V3  0.320   0.601 0.224           1             0 1.083 weak
#>    V4  0.413   0.730 0.289           0             0 0.000 weak
#>    V5  0.338   0.618 0.235           1             0 0.746 weak
#> 
#> Flags are judged against the rest score over the unflagged items.
#> A single significant violation sets 'non-monotone'; with large samples, check n_significant and z_max.
# }
